note: Homestead appeal: the court records only that some rooms 'were rented, while others were occupied by persons who boarded with appellee' and never gives the arrangement a legal character, so the reviewer's 'other' stands; the checker read 'lodging' off the boarding facts, but no lodging or innkeeping doctrine is applied anywhere in the opinion.

The plaintiff was a sub-tenant who occupied the upper portion of the defendant's residence and had paid her rent to the head tenant, and the holding limits the lessor's provisional seizure as against that residential sub-occupant's own goods - a letting question of the same family as the boarding-house lien cases, so it stays relevant.

The holding denies the boarding-house keeper the lien he claimed - chapter 446 of 1860 'confers upon them no greater rights than inn-keepers possessed at common law' and 'the defendant had no right to detain her goods for the debt of her husband' - a pro-boarder result that burdens the keeper, hence adverse; the earlier reviewer appears to have read the statute's protective title (an act for the protection of boarding-house keepers) rather than the disposition.

The only holding is that a lessor who knowingly misrepresented the condition of a house hired for keeping a boarding house cannot recover the rent and the tenant could abandon (judgment for the landlord reversed, new trial); the no-implied-warranty and no-duty-to-disclose rules the reviewer likely relied on are recited and then distinguished, so mixed lacks a second holding and the case resolves adverse to the owner.

Birney follows McIlvaine on the same facts: 'the husband is liable for the board, and as nothing is due from the wife, it follows that her goods can not be detained' - the boarding-house keeper loses the lien he asserted, which is adverse to the owner's side of the letting even though the statute is nominally for keepers' protection.

The owner sued for seven and a half months' rent on a holdover presumption and her judgment was reversed because evidence that the occupant thereafter rented from the co-owner husband and paid him was wrongly excluded; the reviewer probably scored the court's acceptance of the one-dollar two-week letting as favorable, but the disposition runs against the letting owner, so adverse.

The opinion says only that the landlords own a private house at 132 West 87th Street of which the tenant sublet the second and third floors; it never says where the landlords live or in what capacity they hold, so the reviewer's 'unclear' stands and the re-read's non_resident_owner is an inference the record does not carry.

The landlord's summary proceeding was dismissed and the widow tenant who lets fourteen or fifteen of sixteen rooms was held protected by the 1920 act, a restriction on the owner's recovery of possession; the passage exempting premises hired for profit is expressly an assumption ('for the purposes of this appeal, I have assumed'), not a holding, so there is no second side to make it mixed.

The letting party is the executor of a deceased owner's estate and the opinion never states where any owner resided - it describes only the tenant's store-with-rooms occupancy since long before October 1, 1920 - so 'unclear' stands rather than the re-read's inferred non_resident_owner.

Waring rented the West Seneca Street premises to five unrelated individuals sharing kitchen and bath and the stipulated finding is that his 'non-conforming boarding/rooming house use' had been abandoned; the letting is a rooming-house operation, so commercial_operator stands, and nothing in the opinion states his own residence either way.

The court expressly held the innkeeping frame inapplicable - the rule that 'a hotel need not invoke court process to remove a transient occupant' was set aside because 'movant may not be considered a transient' - and placed her under RPAPL 711 as a resident of rooms in a hotel in possession over thirty days, i.e. protected room occupancy rather than innkeeping; the checker's 'other' understates a classification the statute names.

The room was over the defendants' livery stable and was given to their employee as part of his wages, so the letting party is a business occupier of its own commercial building rather than a resident householder; commercial_operator is a defensible reading of that and is not contradicted by the court's words, so the reviewer's value stands.

The single holding is that the defendant's own excise affidavit ('he kept in the house at least three spare beds ... for the accommodation of travelers') established that he kept an inn, so innkeeper's strict liability attached to a diner's lost overcoat 'no matter how slight the entertainment'; the general doctrine that a restaurant or mere lodging-house is not an inn is recited and then held not to save him, so only the adverse side is a holding.

The court's own classification is that a motel is neither a hotel nor a lodging house - 'the distinctions between a "motel" and a "hotel" and a "motel" and a "lodging house" are firmly established in the mind of any reasonable person' - which is exactly what 'other' records; the re-read's 'lodging' is the reading the court rejected.

The court's letting-specific ruling is the boarder exemption - 'the property of a boarder, qua boarder, but not his stock in trade in the house, is protected against seizure for the rent of the boarding-house keeper' - so lodging captures the arrangement the court characterized; the hotel lease and its no-underletting covenant are the backdrop against which that ruling is made.

The court decides by the rent-control categories, not the common-law ones: decontrol survives only where 'the letting is of nonhousekeeping, furnished housing accommodation, located within a single-dwelling unit not used as a rooming or boarding house', and the landlord lost it by 'having rented part of the dwelling unit for housekeeping purposes'; 'other' fits that statutory characterization and nothing in the opinion characterizes a lease.

The court decides only that it is concluded by the prior adjudications upholding the statute and the regulations; the hotel/rooming-house line it quotes comes from Hotel Armstrong, Fablan Studios and Noxon rather than from any classification of an arrangement before it, so the field rightly stays empty and the checker's 'innkeeping' has no support in this opinion.

The petitioners are landlords of a building 'formerly occupied as a rooming house' that was altered into a five-family Class A multiple dwelling and who applied to decontrol all its apartments, with ownership changing during the proceeding; nothing in the record puts any owner in residence, so householder cannot stand and non_resident_owner is what the opinion supports.

The court refused the boarding-house label the village pressed: the code's family definition (which 'may include ... not more than two paying lodgers or boarders') is in 'hopeless conflict' with the two-boarder and boarding-house sections, and the evidence did not show the units were used other than as single housekeeping units, so the arrangement is left uncharacterized as lodging and 'other' stands against the checker's 'lodging'.

The holding imposes a duty on the letting side - 'a boarding-house keeper should be held to the exercise of ordinary and reasonable care in respect of his boarders' goods' and is answerable for his servants' negligence, on the reasoning that he may not have the innkeeper's lien 'without incurring any of his liability'; that liability is the holding and the lien only its premise, so the record is adverse to the keeper.

The disposition exempts the dormitories and food service from taxation outright ('the appellant is exempt from taxation on the parts of its buildings used for the purpose of dormitory and food service facilities'), and the incidental barber shop, bowling alleys and health clubs are exempted too, so there is no restricted side to make it mixed - the tax claim against the letting fails entirely.

The premises are a liquor-licensed hotel whose keeper sued over police interference and the court never applies lodging-house as against innkeeping doctrine - it decides police power only - so 'innkeeping' for a licensed hotel is not contradicted by the court's words, even though the only descriptive phrase is 'thirty-two furnished rooms for lodgers', which is what the checker read as lodging.

On the letting question the owner wins: following Murray v. Charman the court holds that maintaining a private hotel or boarding-house does not violate the covenant, and the injunction expressly excepts service 'to persons who are regular guests of a private hotel or boardinghouse carried on upon said premises'; what was enjoined - the annex run as 'a restaurant and drinking saloon, and nothing else', with no facilities for lodging anyone even one night - is not letting, so it cannot make the record mixed.

The court's own designation is a category of its own - 'the defendant's houses best answer to the designation of a "family hotel"', where 'suites of rooms with board in the general dining room were rented to permanent guests; transient boarders were not received' - which is neither innkeeping (the checker's reading, excluded by the refusal of transients) nor an ordinary lease, so 'other' stands.

Both sides are holdings: the General Term adopted the Special Term's conclusions that the restrictive covenants were not violated and that the owner 'cannot be enjoined from using his buildings for any other purpose or business than dwelling-houses', and separately held that his pre-sale representations estopped him from raising the party-wall to enlarge the family hotel, the alterations already made having been acquiesced in - a recognised freedom to let alongside a real restraint, so mixed stands against the checker's flat adverse.

The action is for rent on a dwelling (a 'store and dwelling') hired for five years, and the court decides the letting questions squarely - no implied covenant that a dwelling house is tenantable, with 'a demise of ready furnished lodgings' named as the exception where a warranty is implied - so it bears on the legal character of paid occupancy of a dwelling and stays relevant.

The dispute is between two men who each claimed the right to let the house to Humphreys and over which of them the year's rent of that dwelling was payable, with a distress and replevin of household goods following; the ruling itself is about being bound by the arbitrators' award, which makes the letting thin, but a contested right to let a dwelling is not 'not a letting case at all', so the human's relevant stands against both machine readings.

The court's holding cuts both ways on one principle - 'the lien and the liability must stand or fall together': the innkeeper gets no lien on the neighbour's horses because their owner was never his guest, but for the same reason he 'was not bound to receive and take care of them' and carries no insurer's liability for them, so a restriction and a freedom are decided together and mixed stands.

The court decides the character of a residential occupancy of another's building and the owner's self-help against it - the arrangement 'did not evidence a tenancy under the owner but an agreement for joint occupancy', and 'even a tenancy at will would have required on part of the landlord terminating the estate some care against loss to the tenant' - the same ground as the service-occupancy cases already in the corpus, so it is not plainly outside the collection even though the occupancy was an incident of the partnership rather than of rent.

The boarding house appears only as the use the tenant made of her leased premises and as the measure of her damages ('have prevented the plaintiff from renting the rooms of her house'); the opinion decides a tenant's standing to sue for a nuisance she came to and never characterizes the arrangement between her and her boarders, so the field rightly stays empty.

Von Behren's lake camp "would be leased ... to all persons desiring to rent it" by the day, with Mrs. Schmitt employed to rent it out and collect the revenues, which is letting as a trade rather than a single absentee lease, so commercial_operator stands.

The court never classified the arrangement: it says only that "the wife took a boarder and let out a furnished room" and decides a matrimonial question, so the field rightly stays empty; the checker read lodging, but that is the reporter's description of the facts, not the court's classification.

The single holding is that the husband "may refuse to have boarders" and has the right "to say what persons, outside of the family, are to share the home" even in a jointly owned house, i.e. the letting was stopped; the reviewer likely read the recognition of a householder's authority over his home as favorable, but under the owner-centred rule the outcome forbids the letting, and the same reviewer coded the parallel report (145 N.Y.S. 976, id 3288237) adverse.

The occupancy at issue is surplus OFFICE space in a bank's own building leased "to various persons for offices" - a commercial lease, not compensated occupancy of a dwelling or rooms - so the record fails the relevance rule despite the citable dictum that "the right to lease one's own property may be regarded as an incident of ownership"; flagged because that dictum is presumably why the record was kept.

Parallel report of Blair v. Blair; the court again only recites that the wife "took a boarder, and let out a furnished room" and classifies nothing, so the empty value stands; the checker's lodging is the fact pattern, not the court's classification.

The holding lets the husband refuse boarders in the jointly owned home and denies the wife a separation for his doing so - a restriction on the letting, and the only holding - so adverse stands and the re-read's mixed has no second holding to rest on.

The only holding annuls the denial of the rooming-house licence as based on "speculative inferences unsupported by the record" and on a misapplication of Correction Law article 23-A; nothing in the opinion upholds a restriction on letting (the remittal for a fair hearing is not a holding against the owner), so mixed has no second side.

The court expressly held the HRA agreement "was not a lease" and that a hotel's permanent tenant "is not necessarily a party to a landlord-tenant relationship, but merely a hotel occupant who has resided there for six months" - a statutory status that is neither lease nor lodging as such, so other stands.

The court found the SRO occupant to be the rent-stabilized permanent tenant "entitled to have a lease issued in his name", so the court's own disposition classifies the arrangement as a lease; the checker's other ignores that express direction.

The court treated the units as transient accommodation held out to the public, "more like hotel rooms than private apartments", and reasoned from the duties for which "innkeepers have long ... been held responsible", so innkeeping stands over the checker's lodging.

Pillsbury is a rent-stabilized loft tenant, not an owner, and the preclusive finding is that she "resided" in the entire two-floor unit with "subletting of part of the space ... always contemplated and permitted", so both halves of non_resident_owner fail on the court's own findings and she is a resident householder letting part of her own home.

The court refused the licensee/participant label and protected her under RPAPL 711's definition of a tenant as "an occupant of one or more rooms in a rooming house", with no lease found or ordered - a bunk in a three-quarter house is lodging, so the value stands against the checker's other.

The court held the whole-house short-term rentals fit neither the Town Code's hotel nor its bed-and-breakfast definition and left the property a residential one-family dwelling; it never called the arrangement a lease, so other stands.

The court frames the compelled arrangement in landlord-tenant terms throughout - the law requires owners to "lease every unit to a bona fide tenant", "compels them to admit persons as tenants with all of the possessory and other rights that that status entails" and "compels owners to be residential landlords" - so lease stands.

The keeper's contract to let rooms with board is enforced and she recovers; the only adverse element is the ordinary mitigation rule that she "could not refuse to rent the rooms to other lodgers, leaving them idle" and still recover the whole price, which limits damages rather than the freedom to let, so favorable stands and there is no second holding for mixed.

The judgment against the boarding-house keeper was affirmed on the holding that he "is liable for the loss of his guest's goods, occasioned through the negligence of his own servants" - a burden imposed on the person letting; the reviewer likely counted the court's refusal to hold him to the innkeeper's insurer liability as the favorable side, but that is reasoning, not a holding, so mixed does not stand.

Judgment for the guest was affirmed on the rule that an innkeeper's liability for baggage "is not terminated the instant the guest pays his bill and leaves the hotel" but continues through an undertaken removal - an extension of liability against the one letting, so the earlier favorable value contradicts the holding under the owner-centred rule.

The innkeeper was held liable for the guest's stolen gold on the holding that his "liability is not limited to property of any particular kind or value", the statutory limiting notice never having been posted; the power to limit liability by notice was unavailable on these facts and so is no second holding, leaving nothing to support mixed.

Mrs. Hamilton "was keeping a boarding house and had from twenty to twenty-five boarders", bought the house and "continued to take boarders" on her separate account - a boarding-house business, which the vocabulary assigns to commercial_operator even though she lived there, so the value stands.

Judgment against the hotel keepers was affirmed on the rule that "inn-keepers are responsible, as depositaries, for effects brought to their house by travelers who lodge therein" unless taken by force; the note that they could have avoided liability by posting the statutory notice did not help them and is not a second holding, so mixed does not stand.

value: An ordinance authorising the mayor to order the occupants of a house of prostitution or assignation to remove, on pain of fine and imprisonment, is a valid exercise of the police power delegated by the city charter; the keeper's ownership of the house is no defence, because the ordinance takes no property but "simply prevents its use by her for purposes inconsistent with public order and morals", and the penalties follow a contradictory hearing, so there is no want of due process.
note: The card carries no earlier human summary and no Holding line, so keep would leave the record without one; this states the opinion's actual holdings - police power delegated by Act 20 of 1882 sec. 8, ownership no exemption, qualified deprivation with due process - in the record's own terms.

The opinion says only that "the defendant leased to the plaintiff a dwelling-house ... for twelve months"; it never states that O'Hern owned the house (the sole hint is the notary calling at his separate residence), so ownership is unestablished and unclear stands over the re-read's non_resident_owner.

The court construed an undefined policy term - "the policy, however, did not define the term 'roomer'" - and held only that "under the particular facts of this case it cannot be said that the exclusionary clause applies"; it never classified the occupancy, so the field rightly stays empty.

The regulated homes furnish "suitable care, for compensation and profit" to persons who require, "in addition to lodging and board, the services of attendants" - a residential care business rather than a lodging relationship as such, so other stands against the checker's lodging.

The plaintiffs occupied a room Mrs. Sledge "sublet" to them out of the leased dwelling, and the holding allocates repair duties between lessor and occupant under Civ. Code art. 2716 - a holding on the legal incidents of a letting of rooms in a dwelling, so it is not plainly a non-letting case.

The lease was of "the house and outbuildings" for "residential purposes only", and the holding is that an owner in possession after the condemnation filing may lease the premises and collect rent from a tenant who cannot dispute her title - a right-to-let holding about a dwelling, so relevance stands.

The court held only that weekly vacation renting did not make the house a "tourist accommodation" and left it a single-family residence; it never characterised the arrangement as a lease, so other stands.

The preliminary injunction against under-30-day rentals was denied outright, on the holdings that "there is no requirement under either the ZR or the certificates of occupancy that the subject buildings be used exclusively for permanent occupancy" and that zoning ambiguity is "resolved in favor of the property owner"; nothing in the opinion upholds a restriction, so there is no second side for mixed.

The lessor who re-let the house and put a second lessee in possession before the month expired was cast in damages to the first lessee; the reviewer likely credited the court's treating a one-month letting as a complete lease, but the holding runs against the owner's freedom to re-let, which is adverse under the owner-centred rule.

The letting of "three rooms on the second story of a tenement house" is the subject of the holding - the evidence showed "only a hiring of the rooms themselves", so control of the stairway stayed with the landlord - which fixes the scope and incidents of a room letting, so relevance stands.

The holdover boarding-house keeper kept possession on the old lease terms and recovered $440 actual damages against the landlord for the sequestration that destroyed her business; the disallowance of exemplary and mental-anguish damages is a damages ruling, not a recognition of the owner's freedom to let, so only the adverse side is a letting holding and mixed does not stand.

The judgment both allows the boarding-house keeper's claim for the sick slave's board and bars the bulk of it under the one-year prescription of art. 3499 for "the claims of innkeepers and such others, for the board and lodging which they furnish" - two holdings pulling opposite ways, so mixed stands, and the re-read's favorable ignores that the plaintiff lost most of his claim.

Goldsmith v. Virgin only overrules an exception of no cause of action, letting a boarding-house keeper sue her LESSOR on the art. 2695 warranty; the reviewer plainly read that holding as burdening the owner-lessor (a pro-lessee outcome), and the opinion decides nothing about freedom to let, so the human 'adverse' is not shown wrong.

1117 Vine Ave is a six-room rooming house run for profit through a resident manager who collects rent under written house rules, so 'commercial_operator' is squarely supported; 'non_resident_owner' is only the other true half of the same facts, not a correction.

Salter v. Zoder turns on whether the occupant of the garage-apartment living quarters was the new owner's tenant and holds he was not ('One may occupy property and pay for such occupancy without being a tenant of anyone') but a licensee - a holding on the legal character of a compensated residential occupancy.

Cheatham v. Bohrer concerns a laborer who rented a room from a tenant of a double dwelling and holds that an owner 'may lease only a portion of his building ... and may set aside any portion as not contemplated for use for dwelling purposes' - a ruling on room-letting and the owner's freedom over what he lets, not incidental colour.

Webster v. Moore decides only that a cost deposit sufficed, that no appeal bond was needed and that a lost writ is not jurisdictional; the tourist-camp rent claim is never reached, so the opinion bears on no letting question at all.

The existing summary matches the opinion in every particular - art. 4592's $50 cap, the concession that only one suitable lock or bolt is required, the rule that a keeper who installs both must keep each safe, the thumb-openable night bolt the guest chose, and affirmance of the full judgment - and is more complete than the re-read's one-liner.

The existing summary tracks the opinion exactly - the Cajun Hostel dealer registration for furnishing sleeping rooms to transients, La. R.S. 47:337.61(2) barring Dore's unfiled defenses and unsworn testimony, the trial court's failure to rule leaving the court of appeal without jurisdiction, and reversal and remand with the tax liability undecided.

Quigley v. Southwick holds the furnished-room-house keeper who lived in the basement and let the other rooms by the week was not an innkeeper and owed only ordinary care, reversing the judgment against her - letting rooms did not saddle the householder with insurer's liability.

Moore v. Aughey affirms judgment for the landlady who let a room at $1 per week, holding that minor repairs such as the loose doorknob 'are by law imposed upon the tenant and not upon the landlord' - the room-letter is relieved on a ground internal to the letting relation.

The YMCA residence is held a 'hotel' under General Business Law 206, but the court construes that penal, common-law-derogating rate-posting statute 'strictly in favor of the hotel' and requires posting only in public rooms, giving the operator judgment on the overcharge counterclaim.

People v. Fisher dismisses the fire-safety-director information because a class-B hotel certificate of occupancy cannot support an inference of the Rules' narrower 90-day transient use - the regulation on transient lodging is narrowed and the prosecution of the operator fails.

Maturi v. Balint holds the proposed motel meets the ordinance's hotel definition and is 'clearly within the permitted uses', ordering the permit issued: if the municipality wants to distinguish types of hotels 'it must do so specifically by ordinance'.

Wolk v. Pittsburgh Hotels enters judgment n.o.v. for the proprietor, holding the character of the occupancy contract governs liability and that he owes no duty to inspect or to answer for a transient guest's window-sill bottle absent knowledge - the letting relation relieves rather than burdens the operator.

Kraus v. Birns declares the Hotel Sherman a hotel under Administrative Code D26-3.22, so 'a permit for a rooming house should not be required of plaintiffs' and the threatened criminal prosecution fails - a licensing restriction on letting is held inapplicable.

People v. Rankin reverses the hotel proprietor's disorderly-person conviction, holding section 899(4) prohibits a course of conduct so guilty knowledge must be proved, rejecting the magistrate's view that strict liability is 'one of the risks of the hotel business'.

People v. Shkilky reverses the landlady's conviction, holding roomers cooking at her common fire do not live 'independently' so the boarding house was never converted into a tenement house, and that single furnished rooms let for days or weeks are not 'homes' under the statute.

Menger v. Pass reverses the injunction and dismisses the bill, holding an automobile tourist court is not a nuisance per se even in an unzoned strictly residential area and that 'such owners possess a constitutional right to use their land for any lawful purpose'.

Dooling's Windy Hill affirms the variance letting the occupant use the premises as a hotel or guest house, finding unnecessary hardship and that the use 'would not be contrary to the public interest' - the zoning bar on letting rooms is lifted.

Matter of Veeder holds an owner in the habit of letting rooms by the week is not thereby a boarding-house keeper carrying on a business: 'A dwelling-house does not lose its character as such merely because its owner occasionally lets rooms by the week.'

Wilson v. Halpin reverses the judgment against the emigrant-boarding-house keeper, holding his established regulation that baggage be left at the bar was reasonable and that the guest who disregarded it bears the loss himself.

Cromwell v. Stephens enjoins the Croton Aqueduct Board from cutting off water over the per-room hotel rate, holding a cheap lodging house letting rooms at twenty-five cents a night without meals is not a 'hotel' within the ordinance - a tax burden on letting is defeated.

Wintermute v. Clark grants the innkeeper a new trial, holding his extraordinary liability 'ceases when the guest pays his bill and leaves the house, with the declared intention of not returning'; the contrary point that receiving all comers made him an innkeeper goes against him, but the operative holding and the disposition relieve the letter.

Hexter v. Knox measures the hotel keeper's damages by the proved rental value of the rooms he was to let - furnished where he had furniture, unfurnished otherwise, varied by season - because the premises were leased 'for hotel purposes ... for the use of such persons as the plaintiff in his business as a hotel keeper should let them to', valuing rather than restricting the letting business.

Ziel v. Borough of Crafton dismisses the mandamus, holding tourist homes fall within the ordinance's own exception that 'in the residence districts the use regulations shall not be held to prevent the renting of rooms or lodgings', and that council could have capped the rooms let but did not.

Davidson v. Ewing gives the landlord ejectment against a week-to-week roomer, the OPA having written that 'since this is a rooming house, we are unable to interfere with the landlord's right to proceed with eviction' - rent-control tenant protection does not reach the room-letting.

Same Veeder liquor-tax ruling reported at 31 Misc. 569: letting one or more rooms to persons outside the family 'would not deprive his house of its character as a dwelling-house', which remains 'for every intent ... a private house' entitled to a dwelling's privacy.

Kynor v. Enggren opens the confessed ejectment judgment, refusing to hold as a matter of law that letting several motel units for extended off-season periods breaches a covenant to use the premises 'as a motel and for no other purpose' - the operator's discretion over how he lets is protected.

Bristol Hotel Co. v. Pegram reverses for the proprietor, holding that absent an express covenant confining the building to apartments he committed no breach and no constructive eviction by letting rooms to transients by the day.

Boom v. City of Utica holds the common council had no nuisance power to remove a sick occupant, since 'a person sick of an infectious or contagious disease, in his own house, or in suitable apartments at a public hotel or boarding house, is not a nuisance' - a nuisance restriction on whom a hotel or boarding house may lodge is denied.

Same Cromwell v. Stephens ruling in its Abbott's report: the eight-story lodging house letting rooms at twenty-five cents per night is 'not chargeable as a hotel' with the higher Croton water tax and the board is enjoined from cutting off the water.

Dixon v. Robbins reverses and dismisses the lodger's complaint, holding the fire-escape statute's word 'hotel' means an inn furnishing food and entertainment and so does not reach a lodging house letting rooms by the day, week or night with no meals, register or public rooms.

Overseers of Crown Point v. Warner holds that 'at common law, any person may erect an inn for the public accommodation, without a license; as the keeping of it is not a franchise, but a lawful trade open to every citizen', only liquor selling requiring a licence, and finds the 'Entertainment'/'Temperance' sign incurred no penalty.

Judgment for the lodger reversed: the boarding-house/inn keeper's own house regulation about depositing baggage was held 'a reasonable and proper regulation' and the keeper not answerable, so the court sided with the keeper's control of his letting establishment.

Montgomery v. Sartirano decides only whether a porter's push on the stairs was within the scope of his employment; the lodging house is the setting and the ejection line is passing dicta, so nothing about compensated occupancy, its character or its regulation is decided - a hotel tort with no letting question.

Bristol Hotel v. Pegram holds that, absent an express covenant, the landlord's renting of rooms to transient day guests was neither a breach nor a constructive eviction of a yearly tenant - the owner's freedom to let transiently was expressly preserved.

Quigley v. Southwick reverses the roomer's judgment and dismisses the complaint: a resident furnished-room keeper letting by the week without meals is a lodging-house keeper liable only for negligence, not an innkeeper, so the court lightened the burden on the householder who lets.

Dawson v. Holiday Pocono: 'the right to lease real estate is an inherent right of ownership which a property owners' association cannot prohibit absent the consent of the affected owners,' and plaintiffs are 'not barred from the short-term rental of their properties' - a restriction on short-term letting struck down.

People v. Shkilky reverses the Tenement House Law conviction and discharges the boarding-house keeper, holding that letting furnished rooms to families who cook in a common kitchen does not convert the house into a tenement house - a regulatory restriction on letting rooms narrowed.

Wood v. City of Brooklyn enjoins the municipal ordinance as void so far as it reaches licensed innkeepers selling to 'their lodgers and lawful travelers,' holding the innkeeper has 'a vested right to the privileges which [his license] confers'; the privilege actually vindicated is the Sunday liquor sale rather than the letting itself, which makes relevance thin, but the court did strike down a municipal restriction on the licensed innkeeping trade, so favorable stands.

The court affirms the temporary injunction against enforcing the Village's short-term-rental ban, holding Hill 'has identified a vested right' because excluding her from grandfathered status 'foreclosed Hill's existing investment use of her property'; the jurisdictional losses on her declaratory action are not holdings about letting.

Orange Stones: the order granting the 20-guest-room hotel/motel zoning permit as a permitted use is affirmed, the zoning officer having erred in refusing it under an ordinance not enacted under the MPC and the board having lacked authority to attach conditions - a zoning obstacle to operating transient lodging removed.

City of New Orleans v. Coles: the City's injunction against renting 705-709 Burgundy for transient occupancy was prescribed under La. R.S. 9:5625, so 'the units of St. Peter Guest House ... acquired and shall enjoy legal non-conforming status' - the transient-rental use survived zoning enforcement.

Herter v. Dwyer reverses the nightly lodger's judgment: the keeper of a lodging house is not charged with an innkeeper's peculiar responsibility and may limit liability by a reasonable posted notice, so the court held for the person letting the rooms.

People v. Drum reverses the hotel manager's disorderly-house conviction, holding the police-decoy registrations insufficient and stressing that 'the keeper of an inn or hotel is bound to receive and accommodate those presenting themselves as guests at his peril' - a criminal restriction on how rooms were let was refused.

In re Veeder holds that an owner 'in the habit of letting rooms by the week to persons who might apply' does not thereby become a boarding-house keeper carrying on a business: 'for every intent it would still be a private house' - letting rooms carried no adverse legal consequence for the householder.

FQCPRQ v. Brandon affirms denial of the neighbours' preliminary injunction against operating 517 Dumaine as a transient rental, appellants having failed to prove six months' vacancy or structural alteration - the guest house's nonconforming letting use was left standing.

Matter of De Angelis directs issuance of a building permit for a 12-unit motel, finding the board's stated reasons insufficient and observing that motels 'cannot be excluded from all areas' - a zoning denial of transient lodging overturned.

Locke v. State holds the trial court abused its discretion in padlocking the second-floor hotel, where Locke lives and rents the remaining rooms to the public, because the Code violations were confined to the first-floor pool halls - a nuisance-closure remedy narrowed so the room letting could continue.

Davis v. Nicholson affirms rejection of the lodger's damage suit, holding 'there is no doubt of the authority of the defendant to retain plaintiff's belongings' as a lodging-house keeper's pledge for seventeen weeks' unpaid room rent - the keeper's statutory remedy against a defaulting lodger was upheld.

LeBlanc v. Palmisano affirms refusal to enjoin the tourist court: the covenant barring commercial construction without the developer's consent 'is not a covenant running with the land, but is a personal covenant,' so neighbours could not stop the short-term lodging use (only the unrelated ten-foot setback was enforced).

Ewing v.
